title: A very different Edinburgh.
summary: A green strip of houses, a volcanic wall, and an enormous ocean. Edinburgh of the Seven Seas is a settlement where the next neighbouring community is about 2,437 kilometres away.

photo.caption: Edinburgh of the Seven Seas, between the Atlantic and the island’s steep volcanic slopes.
photo.alt: Photograph of green fields and houses beneath steep cliffs on Tristan da Cunha.

sections.heading: A village at the edge of the map
sections.text: Start with the photograph: the settlement occupies a narrow patch of relatively level ground, squeezed between steep slopes and the sea. The island’s official account describes its nearest neighbour as Saint Helena, more than two thousand kilometres away. The grand name, Edinburgh of the Seven Seas, belongs to a small community rather than a city. Local people also call it the Settlement. Looking at the houses against the cliffs makes the scale of that isolation easier to grasp than a dot on a world map.

sections.heading: The volcano changed everything
sections.text: In 1961, earthquakes and landslides preceded an eruption close to the settlement. Residents evacuated the island and eventually reached Britain. Their time away lasted through the severe British winter of 1962–63. An advance party returned in 1963, followed by the wider community. The island’s history records a return to homes and livelihoods interrupted by a volcano, rather than the permanent abandonment of a remote outpost.

sections.heading: One detail to keep
sections.text: The surprising part is not simply how far away this place is. It is that the people who lived here chose to come back after leaving. Look again at the photograph: those small buildings are homes in a landscape whose beauty and hazards belong to the same mountain.

title: Trees from another world.
summary: The umbrella-shaped trees of Socotra look improbable, but they are real. Their island home holds an unusually large share of plants and animals found nowhere else on Earth.

photo.caption: A dragon’s blood tree on Socotra’s Dixam plateau. Its umbrella-shaped canopy is a distinctive feature of the island.
photo.alt: Photograph of a dragon’s blood tree with a broad umbrella canopy on a rocky Socotra plateau.

facts.label: Plants found only here
facts.note: Of 825 plant species in UNESCO’s listing

sections.heading: A small archipelago, a large difference
sections.text: Socotra lies in the northwest Indian Ocean, near the Gulf of Aden. UNESCO describes the archipelago as four islands and two rocky islets spread over roughly 250 kilometres. Its World Heritage assessment counts 825 plant species, with 37 percent occurring nowhere else. The corresponding figures are even higher for reptiles and land snails. Biologists call a species endemic when it belongs naturally to a particular place. Here, that word explains why a familiar-looking tree or lizard can have an exceptionally small global home.

sections.heading: The red inside the tree
sections.text: Dragon’s blood trees take their name from a red resin. Their shape is equally memorable: branches spread into a dense, flattened crown above a sturdy trunk. UNESCO’s account of invasive species on Socotra describes local communities’ connections to native plants, including frankincense and dragon’s blood trees. The unusual silhouettes in photographs belong to a lived-in landscape, with people who know and use its plants, rather than an uninhabited botanical display.

sections.heading: Look beyond the famous canopy
sections.text: The tree is an easy starting point, but the wider story includes birds, reptiles, coastal fish and reef-building corals. When an island contains species with no other natural home, protecting a patch of habitat can mean protecting a large part of that species’ entire world. The photograph’s strange shape is the invitation; the distribution of life around it is the real surprise.

title: A forest made of stone.
summary: At Bryce Canyon, thousands of rock spires crowd the slopes like a silent audience. Their sculptor is something small and familiar: water that keeps freezing and thawing.

photo.caption: Hoodoos at sunset in Bryce Canyon National Park, Utah.
photo.alt: Photograph of orange and pale rock spires filling Bryce Canyon at sunset.

facts.label: Cross freezing annually
facts.note: NPS climate account; varies by year

sections.heading: Water works a crack open
sections.text: A hoodoo is an irregular rock pillar left behind as surrounding material wears away. Bryce Canyon has the largest concentration in the world, according to the National Park Service. Here, water seeps into cracks in the rock. When it freezes, it expands; repeated freezing and thawing can widen those cracks until pieces separate. Layers of rock respond differently to weathering, helping create the uneven outlines and narrow waists you can pick out in the photograph.

sections.heading: Cold is part of the machinery
sections.text: The landscape’s warm colours can make it look like a place shaped only by heat. The park’s elevation tells a different story. It ranges from about 6,600 to 9,100 feet above sea level, and an NPS account describes roughly 170 days a year with temperatures on both sides of freezing. That repeated change matters. A permanently frozen crack would not go through the same daily cycle of liquid water entering, freezing, expanding and thawing.

sections.heading: The photograph captures a moment
sections.text: The formations keep changing as weathering and erosion continue. NPS researchers also point out uncertainty about their future as climate conditions shift; a count of freeze-thaw days alone cannot predict exactly what will happen to each spire. Follow one pillar from its broad top down to its narrow base. What looks like a finished sculpture is a temporary shape in a process still under way.

sources.name: NPS: the uncertain future of hoodoos

title: A year before one full turn.
summary: Venus completes a trip around the Sun before it finishes one rotation. But the often-repeated claim that its day is longer than its year needs one small, important distinction.

photo.caption: Venus photographed by NASA’s Mariner 10 spacecraft. The image shows the planet’s cloud cover, not its surface.
photo.alt: Spacecraft photograph of the cloud-covered globe of Venus against black space.

sections.heading: Two clocks on one planet
sections.text: A sidereal day measures one full turn relative to distant stars. On Venus, that takes about 243 Earth days. A year measures an orbit around the Sun, which takes about 225 Earth days. Compare those two clocks and the claim is true: the rotation lasts longer than the orbit. Venus also rotates in the opposite direction from most planets, so an observer on its surface would see the Sun rise in the west and set in the east.

sections.heading: The sunrise clock is different
sections.text: A solar day measures the interval from one sunrise to the next. Rotation and orbital motion both affect it, so it is not identical to the sidereal day. NASA’s fact sheet gives a Venusian solar day of about 116.75 Earth days, usually rounded to 117. That is shorter than the planet’s year. Neither number is a correction to the other: they describe different measurements. The trick is to ask which clock someone means when they say “day.”

sections.heading: What the camera actually saw
sections.text: The photograph comes from Mariner 10, which passed Venus in 1974. You are looking at a world wrapped in clouds. Its calm appearance gives little hint of the conditions below: a dense atmosphere and a surface far hotter than Earth’s. Keep the three numbers separate and the odd fact becomes more interesting than the slogan. One planet can give you a 225-day year, a 243-day rotation, and a 117-day sunrise cycle.

title: Three hearts. Eight busy arms.
summary: An octopus does not need three hearts for three kinds of love. It needs them to move oxygen through a body with gills, blue blood and a remarkably distributed nervous system.

photo.caption: A common octopus photographed in Arrábida Natural Park, Portugal. Other octopus species differ in size and appearance.
photo.alt: Underwater photograph of a common octopus resting among rocks in Portugal.

facts.label: Hearts
facts.note: Two serve the gills; one serves the body

sections.heading: A three-pump arrangement
sections.text: Two hearts push blood through the gills, where it picks up oxygen. A third sends that oxygenated blood around the rest of the body. The blood’s oxygen-carrying protein, haemocyanin, contains copper; our haemoglobin uses iron. That difference helps explain the blue colour of oxygenated octopus blood. The arrangement is a practical solution to keeping an active marine animal supplied with oxygen, rather than three interchangeable copies of a human heart.

sections.heading: The arms do more than follow orders
sections.text: The common octopus has roughly 500 million neurons, according to the Natural History Museum. Many are outside the central brain, including large numbers in the arms. An arm can respond to what it touches without every detail needing a separate instruction from the head. That does not make each arm a separate animal or give the octopus eight human-like minds. It means control is distributed through a body that constantly explores surfaces with flexible, sucker-covered limbs.

sections.heading: Watch the body, not just the face
sections.text: The animal in the photograph is a common octopus, a species studied by researchers and observed by divers. Its soft body, arms and skin are all part of how it interacts with its surroundings. Try following the outline of an arm into the rocks. It is a useful reminder that an animal’s intelligence and circulation do not have to be arranged like ours to support complex behaviour.

title: A mountain in a sugar cube.
summary: The Crab Nebula is a cloud of stellar wreckage. At its centre sits a neutron star: a small remnant whose density makes ordinary comparisons almost stop making sense.

photo.caption: A Hubble observation mosaic of the Crab Nebula. This shows the expanding supernova remnant, not a close-up of neutron-star matter.
photo.alt: Hubble telescope photograph of the Crab Nebula with orange filaments around a blue central cloud.

sections.heading: After the star collapses
sections.text: When some massive stars reach the end of their lives, their cores collapse into neutron stars. A large amount of matter occupies a remarkably small volume. NASA illustrates the density by comparing a sugar cube of neutron-star material with about one trillion kilograms, roughly a mountain’s mass. It is a way to imagine density, not a suggestion that you could scoop up a stable cube and put it on a kitchen scale.

sections.heading: A real example inside the photograph
sections.text: The Crab Nebula is the remnant of a supernova whose light people on Earth recorded in 1054. Its central neutron star spins about thirty times a second. Astronomers call it a pulsar because rotating beams of radiation produce recurring signals as they sweep past us. The photograph shows the much larger cloud around that compact object. The glowing filaments and the small remnant belong to the same stellar event, but they occupy very different scales.

sections.heading: A useful way to look at space pictures
sections.text: Hubble’s view combines observations into a detailed image of the nebula. It is real telescope data, rather than an artist’s imagined scene, but it should not be mistaken for a photograph of the neutron star’s surface. The distinction matters: the beautiful cloud supplies the setting, while measurements of repeating radiation tell astronomers about the fast-spinning object inside. One picture can contain a visible aftermath and an almost invisible engine.

sources.name: NASA: the Crab Nebula and pulsar
